subject: Neurosurgery
title: Traumatic Brain Injury
subtitle: Assessment, skull fractures, concussion, cerebral contusion and traumatic intracranial hemorrhage
sourceNote: Built only from the uploaded NSfomaru Traumatic brain injury lecture. The bank preserves the lecture classifications, numerical thresholds, investigations and management statements as taught, including the wording and framework of its SAH section, without replacing them with external guidelines.

cases.title: Initial Assessment after Road-traffic Trauma
cases.scenario: A 24-year-old man is brought after a road-traffic accident. He opens his eyes to speech, speaks confused words and localizes pain. A skull deformity is suspected.
cases.ar: شاب بعد حادث: eye opening to speech، confused verbal response، وlocalizes pain مع suspected skull deformity.
questions: Calculate the Glasgow Coma Scale score and classify the injury severity.
Which findings in this case are high-risk criteria from the lecture?
Outline the transport and monitoring priorities.
Name the three components of the GCS and their score ranges.
answer: Eye 3 + verbal 4 + motor 5 = GCS 12; this is a moderate injury.
High-risk findings include GCS total below 13 and suspected skull fracture. Other lecture criteria are motor score below 6, signs of basilar fracture and penetrating injury.
Rapid transport with monitoring during transport.
Eye opening 1-4, verbal function 1-5 and motor function 1-6.
cases.trap: Do not classify by the eye response alone; add eye, verbal and motor scores.

cases.title: Severe TBI with Falling Consciousness
cases.scenario: An unconscious trauma patient has a GCS of 7 and requires ventilatory support. CT shows no immediately removable neurosurgical lesion.
cases.ar: مريض trauma فاقد الوعي GCS 7 ومحتاج ventilatory support، والـCT مفيهوش lesion محتاج evacuation فوري.
questions: State the immediate management priorities.
Which two physiological insults must be avoided?
Is ICP monitoring indicated? Give the lecture threshold.
What advantage does an external ventricular drain provide?
State the ICP and CPP goals and the CPP equation.
answer: Assess airway, ventilation and circulation; obtain IV access and intubate if necessary.
Avoid hypoxia and hypotension because they worsen outcome.
Yes. The lecture states ICP monitoring when GCS is below 8.
An EVD permits ICP monitoring and cerebrospinal-fluid drainage.
CPP = MAP - ICP. Keep ICP under 20 mmHg and CPP above 60 mmHg.
cases.trap: Do not focus on ICP while ignoring airway, oxygenation and circulation.
cases.memory: GCS < 8 -> monitor ICP; ICP < 20 and CPP > 60.

cases.title: Raccoon Eyes and CSF Rhinorrhea
cases.scenario: After blunt head trauma, a patient develops periorbital bruising, bruising behind the ear and clear fluid from the nose.
cases.ar: بعد blunt head trauma ظهر raccoon eyes وBattle sign وclear fluid من الأنف.
questions: What is the most likely fracture type?
List the important signs of skull fracture in the lecture.
What test is used for diagnosis?
Outline the management options presented for basal fractures.
List important complications.
answer: Basal (basilar) skull fracture.
Pain, swelling or scalp lump, bruising around the injury, raccoon eyes, Battle sign, CSF leakage from nose or ears and blood from nose, ear or an open wound.
Physical examination and imaging, especially CT scan.
Treatment varies with severity and may include head elevation, drainage of excess or leaking CSF and surgery to repair skull bones/open fractures.
Intracranial hemorrhage, contusion, venous sinus thrombosis, infection/meningitis, paralysis and seizures.
cases.trap: Clear nasal or aural fluid after head trauma should raise suspicion of a basilar fracture.
cases.memory: Raccoon eyes + Battle sign + CSF leak = basilar fracture.

cases.title: Open Depressed Skull Fracture
cases.scenario: A patient has a scalp wound over a depressed segment of skull after direct trauma. CT shows bone fragments pushed toward the brain.
cases.ar: جرح في فروة الرأس فوق depressed segment والـCT يظهر bone fragments pushed toward the brain.
questions: Name the fracture and define it.
How is an open fracture distinguished from a closed fracture?
Why is the open type important?
Outline diagnosis and treatment from the lecture.
What complications should be observed for?
answer: Depressed skull fracture: a break that pushes part of the bone closer to the brain and may involve multiple cracks and fragments.
Open fracture breaks the overlying skin; closed fracture does not.
Open fractures carry a higher risk of infection.
Physical and neurological examination with CT imaging. Treatment may include surgery to repair and reposition skull bones and suture the skin; associated head injuries are treated.
Bleeding, contusion/brain damage, infection, paralysis and seizures.
cases.trap: A depressed fracture is defined by inward displacement, not simply by a visible scalp depression.
cases.memory: Open + depressed -> CT, infection risk and possible surgical repair.

cases.title: Adult with Mild TBI
cases.scenario: After a minor head injury, an adult has headache, nausea, ringing in the ears, fatigue and blurred vision. Brain function is temporarily affected.
cases.ar: بعد minor head injury: headache، nausea، tinnitus، fatigue وblurred vision مع temporary brain dysfunction.
questions: What is the diagnosis and definition?
List the physical symptoms in adults mentioned in the lecture.
What GCS range corresponds to mild injury?
Enumerate potential complications.
answer: Concussion, also called mild traumatic brain injury, is a head injury that temporarily affects brain functioning.
Headache, nausea, vomiting, fatigue or drowsiness, ringing in the ears and blurry vision.
Post-traumatic headache, post-traumatic vertigo, persistent post-concussive symptoms, effects of multiple brain injuries and second-impact syndrome.
cases.trap: A normal scan does not exclude concussion or post-concussion syndrome in the lecture.
cases.memory: Concussion = temporary dysfunction; PCS may last weeks or months.

cases.title: Child after Head Injury
cases.scenario: A young child becomes irritable and listless after a fall, vomits, loses balance and loses interest in favorite toys.
cases.ar: طفل بعد fall أصبح irritable وlistless مع vomiting وloss of balance وعدم اهتمام بالألعاب.
questions: What diagnosis should be considered?
List the pediatric features from the lecture.
Which later syndrome may occur if symptoms persist for weeks or months?
How is that syndrome diagnosed?
answer: Concussion/mild TBI.
Dazed appearance, irritability, excessive crying, vomiting, listlessness and easy tiring, loss of balance, altered eating or sleeping patterns and lack of interest in favorite toys.
Post-concussion syndrome.
PCS is diagnosed clinically from medical history, symptom type and whether symptoms began before or after the head injury; the lecture states it does not show on scans or blood tests.
cases.trap: Children may present with behavioral change rather than a detailed symptom history.
cases.memory: Irritability + vomiting + balance or behavior change after trauma -> consider concussion.

cases.title: Persistent Symptoms after Concussion
cases.scenario: Six weeks after a concussion, a patient has persistent headache, dizziness, photophobia, tinnitus, poor sleep, irritability and impaired concentration.
cases.ar: بعد concussion بست أسابيع ما زال عنده headache، dizziness، photophobia، tinnitus، sleep problems وpoor concentration.
questions: What is the diagnosis?
Classify the symptoms into physical, psychological and cognitive groups.
How is the diagnosis established according to the lecture?
Outline management.
answer: Post-concussion syndrome (PCS).

Physical: headache, dizziness, nausea, light/noise sensitivity, tinnitus, visual disturbance, fatigue and altered smell/taste. Psychological: depression, anxiety, irritability, low energy, loss of interest, sleep/appetite change and emotional outbursts. Cognitive: poor concentration, forgetfulness, difficulty learning/remembering and reasoning difficulty.
Clinical diagnosis using history, symptom pattern and timing; PCS does not show on scans or blood tests.
There is no specific curative treatment in the lecture; supportive strategies are used and symptoms usually improve gradually over time.
cases.trap: Do not dismiss PCS because imaging is normal.
cases.memory: PCS = persistent physical + psychological + cognitive symptoms.

cases.title: Frontal Hemorrhagic Contusions after Trauma
cases.scenario: A road-traffic victim develops impaired consciousness, vomiting and focal weakness. CT shows bilateral frontal hemorrhagic contusions that enlarge on repeat imaging.
cases.ar: بعد RTA: impaired consciousness وvomiting وfocal weakness، والـCT يظهر bilateral frontal hemorrhagic contusions بتكبر في repeat CT.
questions: Define cerebral contusion and state common sites.
Explain coup and contrecoup distribution.
Which clinical features are indications for head CT in the lecture?
Outline initial management.
State seizure prophylaxis and ICP management.
answer: A cerebral contusion is a hemorrhagic injury causing permanent damage to cerebral tissue; it commonly affects frontal and temporal lobes.
Coup injury is beneath the impact; contrecoup injury is opposite the impact.
Impaired consciousness or loss of consciousness, focal neurological findings, persistent vomiting, seizures and abnormal GCS.
Assess airway, ventilation and circulation, obtain IV access, intubate if needed and avoid hypoxia and hypotension.
Seizure prophylaxis for seven days. Raised ICP is managed with sedation, diuresis and hypertonic saline; monitor ICP when GCS is below 8.
cases.trap: Contusions can progress and expand, so deterioration requires reassessment and repeat imaging.
cases.memory: Frontal/temporal hemorrhagic lesions can blossom after the first CT.

cases.title: Contusion with Mass Effect
cases.scenario: A patient with a temporal contusion deteriorates neurologically. CT shows a 24-cc lesion, cisternal compression and 7-mm midline shift despite treatment for raised ICP.
cases.ar: Temporal contusion 24 cc مع neurological deterioration، cistern compression وmidline shift 7 mm رغم علاج raised ICP.
questions: List the surgical indications present in this case.
Enumerate all surgical-removal indications stated in the lecture.
What operation may be required?
When may decompressive craniectomy be considered?
answer: Present indications: progressive neurological deterioration, mass effect/cisternal compression, unresponsive raised ICP, midline shift over 5 mm and temporal contusion over 20 cc.
Progressive deterioration, CT mass effect, raised ICP unresponsive to treatment, midline deviation over 5 mm, cistern compression and temporal contusion over 20 cc.
Immediate craniotomy with evacuation/removal of the contusion may be required.
In extreme cases with ICP unresponsive to usual measures; the lecture notes lower mortality but more survivors in a vegetative state.
cases.trap: The thresholds in this lecture are midline shift >5 mm and temporal contusion >20 cc.
cases.memory: Deterioration + mass effect + refractory ICP -> surgical evaluation.

cases.title: Second Head Injury before Recovery
cases.scenario: An athlete sustains a second concussion before the symptoms of the first concussion have resolved and then develops rapid catastrophic brain swelling.
cases.ar: لاعب أخذ second concussion قبل ما symptoms of the first injury تختفي وحدث rapid catastrophic brain swelling.
questions: Name and define the syndrome.
Why is the timing of the second injury important?
Which earlier concussion complication list includes this syndrome?
State the key prevention message supported by the definition.
answer: Second-impact syndrome: rapid catastrophic brain swelling after a second concussion before symptoms of the first have subsided.
The brain has not recovered from the first concussion when the second impact occurs.
It is listed among the potential complications of concussion.
Avoid a second head impact/return to exposure while symptoms from the first concussion persist.
cases.trap: The defining feature is the second concussion before recovery, not simply two remote concussions.
cases.memory: Second impact before symptom resolution -> catastrophic swelling.

cases.title: Acute Subdural Hematoma
cases.scenario: After severe blunt trauma, a patient develops immediate severe headache, vomiting, slurred speech and contralateral weakness. CT shows a crescent-shaped extra-axial collection with midline shift.
cases.ar: بعد severe blunt trauma ظهر severe headache وvomiting وslurred speech وweakness، والـCT يظهر crescent collection مع midline shift.
questions: What is the diagnosis and timing category?
List the symptoms in the lecture.
State common risk factors.
What is the main operation for a large acute lesion?
List major untreated and postoperative complications.
answer: Acute subdural hematoma, developing within minutes to hours.

Persistent severe headache, nausea/vomiting, dysarthria, visual change, dizziness, gait/balance difficulty and unilateral weakness; severe features include seizures, respiratory problems, loss of consciousness and coma.
Older age, infancy/shaken baby syndrome, contact sports, anticoagulants, hemophilia and alcohol use disorder.
Craniotomy with removal of the hematoma.
Untreated: herniation, coma and death, repeated bleeding and seizures. Surgery risks include further bleeding, infection, DVT, seizures and stroke.
cases.trap: A crescent-shaped collection is the classic SDH pattern in the lecture comparison images.

cases.title: Elderly Patient with Personality Change
cases.scenario: An elderly patient taking blood thinners presents weeks after a minor head injury with memory loss, disorientation, personality change and unsteady gait.
cases.ar: مريض كبير على anticoagulants بعد minor trauma بأسابيع عنده memory loss، disorientation، personality change وunsteady gait.
questions: What is the most likely diagnosis?
Why are older people at greater risk according to the lecture?
What conditions may this presentation mimic?
Outline diagnosis and the main operation.
What postoperative arrangement is commonly left in place?
answer: Chronic subdural hematoma.
Age-related brain shrinkage widens the space between skull and brain, stretching veins and making them more likely to tear.
Brain tumor, stroke or dementia.
Clinical/neurological assessment and brain imaging; burr-hole drainage is the main treatment for chronic SDH.
A drain is often left for several days to permit continued drainage.
cases.trap: Chronic SDH can look like dementia or stroke; always ask about remote trauma and anticoagulants.
cases.memory: Chronic SDH -> weeks-months -> burr holes + drain.

cases.title: Lucid Interval followed by Deterioration
cases.scenario: A young man briefly loses consciousness after temporal trauma, becomes alert for several hours, then deteriorates with severe headache, vomiting and unilateral pupil enlargement. CT shows a biconvex collection.
cases.ar: شاب بعد temporal trauma فقد الوعي، ثم lucid interval، وبعدها deterioration مع severe headache وunilateral dilated pupil والـCT biconvex collection.
questions: What is the diagnosis?
Where is the blood located and what is the classic source?
Describe the typical symptom pattern and CT appearance.
Which findings indicate surgery?
State the preferred operation.
answer: Epidural/extradural hematoma.
Between the skull and dura mater; classically arterial bleeding from the middle meningeal artery associated with skull fracture.
Loss of consciousness, an alert/lucid interval, then renewed loss of consciousness and neurological decline. CT shows a biconvex/lentiform hyperdense collection that does not cross sutures.
Neurological deterioration, pupil asymmetry, significant hematoma or midline shift and CT signs predicting herniation; rapid unilateral pupil dilation is an emergency.
Craniotomy and hematoma evacuation.
cases.trap: Not every EDH has the classic lucid interval, but when present it is highly suggestive.
cases.memory: EDH = artery + lens + lucid interval -> emergency craniotomy.

cases.title: Small Stable Epidural Hematoma
cases.scenario: A neurologically stable patient has a small epidural collection causing only mild symptoms and no significant pressure effect.
cases.ar: مريض neurologically stable عنده small EDH وmild symptoms بدون significant pressure effect.
questions: Can non-operative management be considered according to the lecture?
What monitoring is required?
Which changes would move the patient toward surgery?
List surgery complications presented in the lecture.
answer: Yes. Small bleeds without brain pressure and with mild symptoms may be managed conservatively.
Close clinical monitoring with repeat head CT scans to confirm healing.
Neurological deterioration, pupil asymmetry, significant size/midline shift or CT prediction of herniation.
Infection, bleeding, seizures, brain or spinal-cord damage, herniation, coma or death.
cases.trap: Conservative treatment requires close observation and repeat imaging, not discharge without follow-up.
cases.memory: Small stable EDH -> observe + repeat CT; deterioration -> surgery.

cases.title: Acute Severe Headache with Subarachnoid Blood
cases.scenario: Following head trauma, a patient develops sudden severe headache, neck stiffness, vomiting, photophobia and reduced alertness. CT shows blood in the subarachnoid spaces.
cases.ar: بعد head trauma حصل sudden severe headache مع neck stiffness، vomiting، photophobia وreduced alertness، والـCT يظهر subarachnoid blood.
questions: What is the diagnosis and anatomical definition?
List the symptoms stated in the lecture.
What diagnostic modalities are shown on the lecture diagnosis slide?
Outline the management framework presented in the lecture.
How is hyponatremia handled in the lecture?
answer: Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage: bleeding in the space below the thin layers that cover and protect the brain.

Thunderclap/severe headache, reduced consciousness, nausea/vomiting, stiff neck, sudden weakness, confusion/irritability, dizziness, photophobia, neck/shoulder aches, numbness, seizures and visual change.
CT-based imaging is illustrated, with lumbar puncture, ABG and sodium assessment listed.

Initial stabilization with airway/breathing, strict bed rest and blood-pressure management; secure the bleeding source with coiling or clipping when applicable; prevent complications with nimodipine, ICP management and seizure prevention.
Immediate correction with hypertonic saline; the lecture advises avoiding fluid restriction and prioritizing saline resuscitation.
cases.trap: The lecture combines traumatic SAH with management principles also used when an aneurysmal source is present; reproduce its framework as taught.
cases.memory: SAH = blood in subarachnoid space + sudden severe headache.

cases.title: Identify the Intracranial Bleed
cases.scenario: Four CT patterns are presented: a lentiform extra-axial collection, a crescentic extra-axial collection, blood tracking through sulci/cisterns and a rounded intraparenchymal collection.
cases.ar: أربع CT patterns: lentiform، crescentic، blood in sulci/cisterns، وrounded intraparenchymal bleed.
questions: Match each pattern to its diagnosis.
Compare the usual source of EDH and SDH.
Which lesion commonly has a lucid interval?
Which lesion may be acute, subacute or chronic?
State the emergency operation for a large EDH and the main operations for acute and chronic SDH.
answer: Lentiform = EDH; crescentic = SDH; sulci/cisterns = SAH; rounded intraparenchymal = intracerebral/intraparenchymal hemorrhage.
EDH is usually arterial, classically middle meningeal artery; SDH is usually venous from bridging veins in the lecture comparison.
EDH.
SDH.
Large EDH: craniotomy and evacuation. Acute SDH: craniotomy. Chronic SDH: burr holes with a drain.
cases.trap: Shape and anatomical compartment are more reliable than memorizing the name alone.

coreShorts.q: Enumerate the high-risk transport criteria listed for TBI.
a: Skull deformity or suspected skull fracture.

coreShorts.q: Name the components and score ranges of the Glasgow Coma Scale.
Write the eye-opening score in the GCS.
Write the verbal-response score in the GCS.
Write the motor-response score in the GCS.
Classify TBI severity by GCS.
Enumerate the Glasgow Outcome Scale categories.
Differentiate penetrating and non-penetrating TBI.
a: Penetrating/open TBI: an object pierces the skull and enters brain tissue.
Non-penetrating/closed TBI: external force moves the brain inside the skull without penetration.

coreShorts.q: Enumerate the closed-TBI examples named in the lecture.
Differentiate mild, moderate and severe TBI by the lecture descriptions.
a: Mild: temporary symptoms such as headache, confusion, memory and concentration problems.
Moderate: more prolonged symptoms, including loss of consciousness over 30 minutes but under 24 hours.
Severe: loss of consciousness over 24 hours, possible coma and severe neurological deficits.

coreShorts.q: Enumerate the types of skull fracture.
Differentiate open and closed skull fractures.
a: Closed: overlying skin remains intact and is more common.
Open: skin is broken over the fracture and infection risk is higher.

coreShorts.q: List important clinical signs of a skull fracture, especially a basilar fracture.
a: Clear CSF from nose or ears.
Blood from nose, ear or an open wound.

coreShorts.q: Enumerate complications associated with skull fracture.
State diagnosis and management of a linear skull fracture in the lecture.
a: Diagnosis: physical examination and CT imaging.
Most linear fractures need no specific treatment and heal on their own.
Observe for complications such as seizures and treat associated head injury.

coreShorts.q: Outline treatment options for basal, depressed and diastatic skull fractures.
a: Drain excess or leaking CSF when required.
Surgical repair/repositioning of skull bones and closure of open wounds according to severity.

coreShorts.q: Define concussion.
coreShorts.a: A concussion, or mild TBI, is a head injury that temporarily affects brain functioning.

coreShorts.q: List physical symptoms of concussion in adults.
List concussion symptoms in children.
a: Change in eating or sleeping patterns.
Loss of interest in favorite toys.

coreShorts.q: Enumerate potential complications of concussion.
Define post-concussion syndrome and classify its symptom groups.
a: Symptoms after concussion lasting weeks or months.

coreShorts.q: How is PCS diagnosed and managed according to the lecture?
a: It does not show on scans or blood tests; diagnosis uses medical history, symptoms and timing relative to head injury.
There is no specific curative treatment in the lecture.
Supportive strategies are used and most patients improve gradually.

coreShorts.q: Define cerebral contusion and state its common sites.
a: A hemorrhagic lesion causing permanent damage to cerebral tissue.
Begins in cortical areas, often at gyri crests.
May extend into subcortical white matter in severe injury.

coreShorts.q: Explain coup and contrecoup injuries.
a: Coup contusion lies beneath the impact.
Contrecoup contusion lies opposite the impact.
Multiple focal contusions may have a salt-and-pepper appearance.

coreShorts.q: List indications for head CT in the lecture.
What is the role of MRI in acute TBI according to the lecture?
a: MRI is not indicated in acute TBI management.
The lecture describes signal appearances if MRI is performed, including petechial hemorrhages on FLAIR.

coreShorts.q: Outline the initial management priorities in cerebral contusion/TBI.
When is ICP monitoring performed and what is the advantage of EVD?
a: The lecture states ICP monitoring when GCS is below 8.

coreShorts.q: Define CPP and state the treatment targets.
State seizure prophylaxis and medical treatment of raised ICP in cerebral contusion.
Enumerate indications for surgical removal of a cerebral contusion.
Define second-impact syndrome.
coreShorts.a: Rapid catastrophic brain swelling after a second concussion occurs before symptoms of the first concussion have subsided.

coreShorts.q: Classify SDH by timing and state the main operations.
a: Acute: minutes to hours; main treatment for a large acute SDH is craniotomy.
Subacute: hours to days or even weeks.
Chronic: weeks to months; main treatment is burr-hole drainage with a drain often left for several days.

coreShorts.q: State the key features of EDH.
a: Usually arterial, classically middle meningeal artery torn with skull fracture.
Often temporal and more common in young patients.
CT is biconvex/lentiform and does not cross sutures.

coreShorts.q: Outline the management framework for SAH shown in the lecture.
a: Initial stabilization: airway/breathing, strict bed rest and blood-pressure management.
Secure the source by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping when applicable.
Seizure prevention; treat hyponatremia with hypertonic saline and avoid fluid restriction.

detailedShorts.q: What should occur during transport of a high-risk TBI patient?
detailedShorts.a: Rapid transport with patient monitoring.

detailedShorts.q: A patient opens eyes to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds and withdraws from pain. Calculate the GCS.
detailedShorts.a: E2 + V2 + M4 = 8, a severe injury.

detailedShorts.q: A patient opens eyes spontaneously, is oriented and obeys commands. Calculate the GCS.
detailedShorts.a: E4 + V5 + M6 = 15, a mild injury by GCS classification.

detailedShorts.q: What does Glasgow Outcome Scale score 4 mean?
detailedShorts.a: Moderate disability: significant disability but able to live independently.

detailedShorts.q: What does Glasgow Outcome Scale score 2 mean?
detailedShorts.a: Persistent vegetative state: not conscious, although eyes may be open and may track movement.

detailedShorts.q: Give three examples of penetrating objects from the lecture.
detailedShorts.a: Bullet, shrapnel and bone fragment.

detailedShorts.q: What is a contusion in the closed-TBI list?
detailedShorts.a: A bruise of brain tissue.

detailedShorts.q: What is diffuse axonal injury in the lecture definition?
detailedShorts.a: Widespread damage to nerve fibers in the brain.

detailedShorts.q: What duration of loss of consciousness is described for moderate TBI?
detailedShorts.a: More than 30 minutes but less than 24 hours.

detailedShorts.q: What duration is described for severe TBI?
detailedShorts.a: Loss of consciousness for more than 24 hours, potentially with coma and severe neurological deficit.

detailedShorts.q: What is the most common skull-fracture type?
detailedShorts.a: Linear fracture.

detailedShorts.q: Define a depressed skull fracture.
detailedShorts.a: A break that pushes part of the skull bone closer to the brain and may include multiple cracks/fragments.

detailedShorts.q: Define a basilar skull fracture.
detailedShorts.a: A break in bones at the base of the skull, including bones behind the face and internal skull-base bones.

detailedShorts.q: Define a diastatic fracture.
detailedShorts.a: Separation of cranial sutures.

detailedShorts.q: Define a complex skull fracture.
detailedShorts.a: A fracture involving several fracture types or multiple areas of fractured bone.

detailedShorts.q: List neurological symptoms that may occur when a skull fracture affects the brain.
a: Nausea/vomiting, confusion, slurred speech, visual loss, sensory loss, impaired balance/coordination and fatigue.

detailedShorts.q: What is the usual treatment of an uncomplicated linear fracture?
detailedShorts.a: No specific fracture treatment; it generally heals on its own while associated injury and complications are observed.

detailedShorts.q: Why may head elevation be used in basal/depressed/diastatic fracture care?
detailedShorts.a: It is one of the supportive treatment measures listed in the lecture.

detailedShorts.q: Is concussion necessarily associated with permanent loss of brain function?
detailedShorts.a: No. The lecture defines it as temporary impairment of brain functioning.

detailedShorts.q: Name two common post-traumatic symptoms after concussion.
detailedShorts.a: Post-traumatic headache and post-traumatic vertigo.

detailedShorts.q: List six physical symptoms of PCS.
a: Persistent headache, dizziness, nausea, light sensitivity, noise sensitivity, tinnitus, blurred/double vision, fatigue or altered smell/taste.

detailedShorts.q: List psychological symptoms of PCS.
a: Depression, anxiety, irritability, low energy, loss of interest, sleep problems, appetite change and emotional outbursts.

detailedShorts.q: List cognitive symptoms of PCS.
a: Reduced concentration, forgetfulness, difficulty remembering or learning new information and reasoning difficulty.

detailedShorts.q: Why can a normal scan coexist with PCS?
detailedShorts.a: The lecture states that PCS does not appear on scans or blood tests and is diagnosed clinically.

detailedShorts.q: Describe the tissue effects around a hemorrhagic contusion.
a: Local hemorrhage may cause ischemia and edema, tissue destruction, neuronal necrosis, cavitation and reactive gliosis.

detailedShorts.q: What frequency of contusion progression is quoted in the lecture?
List mechanisms/causes of cerebral contusion from the lecture.
a: Road-traffic accidents, falls, aggression, recreation/sports injury, cyclists, domestic violence, child abuse and blast injury.

detailedShorts.q: Which laboratory tests are listed for trauma evaluation?
a: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, INR and toxicology; ABG for intubated patients or respiratory distress.

detailedShorts.q: Which plain radiographs are suggested in the trauma workup?
detailedShorts.a: Entire spine, chest and pelvis, plus other obviously involved bones.

detailedShorts.q: What may multiple focal contusions look like?
detailedShorts.a: A salt-and-pepper appearance.

detailedShorts.q: Why are hypoxia and hypotension important in TBI?
detailedShorts.a: The lecture states both are detrimental to outcome and must be avoided.

detailedShorts.q: What does an EVD add beyond pressure monitoring?
detailedShorts.a: It allows drainage of cerebrospinal fluid.

detailedShorts.q: For how long is seizure prophylaxis started in cerebral contusion?
detailedShorts.a: Seven days.

detailedShorts.q: Name three medical measures for increased ICP in the lecture.
detailedShorts.a: Sedation, diuresis and hypertonic saline.

detailedShorts.q: What two numerical CT thresholds are given for surgery?
detailedShorts.a: Midline shift more than 5 mm and temporal contusion volume greater than 20 cc.

detailedShorts.q: List long-term complications/effects associated with brain contusion.
a: Seizures, hydrocephalus, anosmia, disability, coma/death, cognitive impairment, personality change and loss of school/work time.

detailedShorts.q: What happens to the brain in second-impact syndrome?
detailedShorts.a: It swells rapidly and catastrophically after a second concussion before recovery from the first.

detailedShorts.q: Where is a subdural hematoma located?
detailedShorts.a: Between dura and arachnoid, near the brain.

detailedShorts.q: State the timing of acute, subacute and chronic SDH.
detailedShorts.a: Acute minutes-hours; subacute hours-days or even weeks; chronic weeks-months.

detailedShorts.q: List symptoms of chronic SDH highlighted in the lecture.
detailedShorts.a: Memory loss, disorientation and personality change.

detailedShorts.q: Why are babies at risk of SDH?
detailedShorts.a: Weak neck muscles provide less protection from head trauma; shaken baby syndrome is mentioned.

detailedShorts.q: List non-age risk factors for SDH.
detailedShorts.a: Contact sports, blood thinners, hemophilia and alcohol use disorder.

detailedShorts.q: What history is important in assessing SDH?
detailedShorts.a: Symptoms, mechanism and timing of injury, underlying conditions and medications.

detailedShorts.q: What is the main treatment for acute SDH?
detailedShorts.a: Craniotomy with temporary skull removal to access and remove the hematoma.

detailedShorts.q: What is the main treatment for chronic SDH?
detailedShorts.a: One or more burr holes with a drain often kept for several days.

detailedShorts.q: When may SDH be observed rather than operated?
detailedShorts.a: When small and causing few or no symptoms; rest, medication and observation may be sufficient.

detailedShorts.q: List major complications of untreated large SDH.
detailedShorts.a: Brain herniation, repeated bleeding, seizures, coma and death.

detailedShorts.q: Where is EDH located and what usually causes it?
detailedShorts.a: Between skull and dura; usually an artery torn by skull fracture, classically middle meningeal artery.

detailedShorts.q: State age/sex patterns in EDH from the lecture.
detailedShorts.a: More common in young people, four times more likely in males, and rare before age 2 or after age 60.

detailedShorts.q: What proportion and location statements are quoted for EDH?
detailedShorts.a: Up to 10% of head injuries; about 75% of adult EDHs are temporal.

detailedShorts.q: List other early symptoms of EDH.
detailedShorts.a: Severe headache, nausea/vomiting, unilateral enlarged pupil, confusion, slurred speech, dizziness and unilateral weakness.

detailedShorts.q: What late features may occur as EDH pressure rises?
detailedShorts.a: Seizures, breathing problems, loss of brain function, coma and death.

detailedShorts.q: List the lecture indications for EDH surgery.
detailedShorts.a: Neurological deterioration, pupil asymmetry, significant size/midline shift and CT findings predicting herniation.

detailedShorts.q: How is a small stable EDH followed?
detailedShorts.a: Close monitoring with repeat CT scans to confirm resolution/healing.

detailedShorts.q: Where does SAH occur?
detailedShorts.a: In the subarachnoid space below the thin protective layers covering the brain.

detailedShorts.q: What is the main symptom and what meningeal features may accompany SAH?
detailedShorts.a: Sudden severe/thunderclap headache with stiff neck and photophobia; nausea/vomiting may occur.

detailedShorts.q: How does the lecture approach hyponatremia in SAH?
detailedShorts.a: Immediate hypertonic saline, generally avoiding fluid restriction; saline resuscitation is prioritized because CSW and SIADH may be difficult to distinguish.

detailedShorts.q: Match CT shape to EDH, SDH, SAH and intraparenchymal hemorrhage.
detailedShorts.a: EDH lentiform/biconvex; SDH crescentic; SAH tracks in sulci/fissures/cisterns; intraparenchymal hemorrhage is within brain tissue and often rounded.
